Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-04 14:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Recording id: ff-20260504-rm-week3
Links referenced: bench CSV (https://redwood.app/bench/rm-week3-results), week-3 deck (https://redwood.app/decks/rm-week3), security pack (https://redwood.app/sec/rm-pack)

[00:00] Alex (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate the time. quick run through agenda — Samira will go over the bench readout, then we'll talk routing and then next steps.
[00:18] Tom (CTO) - Rivermark: sounds good, we've got Maya and Devon on. excited to see the numbers.
[00:26] Samira (SE): ok so slide one, high level, we ran identical model snapshots (v1.3) against your test load generator and compared Redwood hosted path vs your incumbent (CurrentStack). the key numbers: p50 for Redwood was ~58ms end-to-end vs 120ms for CurrentStack, p95 was 220ms vs 420ms respectively, throughput at target‑latency (200ms) was about 2.2k rps for Redwood vs 1.5k rps for incumbent.
[00:48] Maya (Lead ML Eng) - Rivermark: uh wow those deltas look decent, um can you remind me if those include network time?
[00:55] Samira (SE): yes it's end-to-end from your loadgen inside the lab to response completion; we also ran an intra-region isolate test to remove public internet — those isolated runs still show a 40–50% improvement.
[01:10] Devon (SRE): there were some spikes on our end yesterday, we saw jitter up to 180ms intermittently, not sure if that's network or test harness.
[01:18] Alex (AE): right, and that's one of the things we flagged — your VPC peering config had MTU mismatch in the earlier test which can create re-transmits. Devon will share the network logs.
[01:28] Devon (SRE) - Rivermark: will do — I'll pull the syslogs and tcpdump and drop them in the sheet.
[01:34] Samira (SE): back to bench, we also toggled KV cache on prefix matches — with cache enabled we saw p95 drop from 220ms to 160ms on average for many of your prompts, because the KV hit rate was ~68% on our sample prompts. without cache the incumbent couldn't keep KV locality as efficient in their config.
[01:55] Maya: are you using the same quantization profiles? like 8-bit q4 or something?
[02:01] Samira: yes, we used q4b for this run, same as the incumbent's profile that you shared. we also tried a more aggressive q2 variant and saw cost savings but a small accuracy bump that you flagged in evals, so we kept q4b for parity.
[02:15] Tom: curious about tail latency — you said p99s were still high?
[02:20] Samira: p99s were around 600ms in our runs, and we traced most of that to cold KV cache misses combined with occasional GC pauses on the lab's loadgen. we recommended warmed caches, and Samira (laughs) ok that was me saying Samira recommended a warmup pass and continuous batching policy.
[02:40] Speaker 5 (transcription artifact): mmhm yeah
[02:44] Alex: (overlapping) the important part is that with routing fallbacks enabled — we can serve to a cheaper variant if the high‑perf cluster is saturated — responses remain within your 300ms SLO for 98% traffic. basically graceful degradation.
[03:00] Maya: how much do the routing fallbacks cost compared to your primary?
[03:04] Samira: ballpark, 30–40% less per-token on fallback variants; tradeoff is slightly higher generation time and, depending on prompt, slight divergence. we can show per-route unit economics in the sheet.
[03:16] Tom: security check — our security team will need KMS integration and audit logs before Private deployment. where are you on SOC2?
[03:24] Alex: Redwood is SOC2 Type II certified, we have a KMS integration path and HSM options for Private. I'll share the security pack link in the notes.
[03:33] Devon: SSO — we need SAML/SCIM provisioning for RBAC sync.
[03:37] Alex: yep we support SAML and SCIM, and can demo the provisioning flows if you'd like.
[03:42] Samira: another experimental run — we tried continuous batching with a 30ms batching window and observed throughput improvements of ~18% with negligible p50 impact. if you can accept a small batching window in your latency SLO, throughput headroom improves considerably.
[04:00] Maya: that sounds promising. our app pattern has a mix — short prompts (user intent) and long prompts (context). the long ones dominate tokens but short ones dominate QPS. how do you recommend splitting?
[04:12] Samira: route short prompts to a low-latency partition with tighter batching (10–15ms) and long prompts to a throughput partition with 30–50ms windows; Redwood tooling can auto-classify by route.
[04:24] Tom: on the incumbent we saw throughput collapse at tail loads around 2k rps; your numbers show 2.2k sustaining — what's the buffer headroom for traffic spikes?
[04:32] Samira: we observed about 20% headroom before p95 crossed 300ms; and autoscale policies we proposed keep a warm pool for sudden spikes. dedicated slots would increase that headroom to ~40% with guaranteed burst capacity.
[04:45] Alex: on pricing, dedicated slot cost depends on commit term — we'll follow up with a committed pricing sheet.
[04:52] Maya: any oddities in the logs — like tokenization mismatch or model outputs being different?
[04:56] Samira: outputs matched within tolerance on our evals; we saw one prompt family with hallucination variance when we used q2 aggressive quant; at q4b parity it's fine.
[05:08] Devon: network — I'll note we saw long tail jitter when we ramped concurrent connections to 4k; suspect our NAT gateway config in the lab.
[05:16] Alex: ok we'll set up a short triage with infra, copy of logs to the bench sheet.
[05:20] Tom: curious — how much integration work is required to move to Private? we are regulatory constrained so Private likely.
[05:27] Alex: Private has two tracks — VPC-hosted private (control plane managed) or full on‑prem. for VPC we handle control plane; you keep KMS and network. typical lift is a few weeks for SSO/KMS and network peering; on‑prem is heavier. we'll circulate the checklist.
[05:40] Maya: can we get the per-route p95 numbers? the slide deck had an aggregate.
[05:44] Samira: yes, per-route details are in the CSV link I uploaded — p95 for route A (short intents) was 140ms, route B (long context) was 340ms when ran against the incumbent at the same concurrency. Redwood was 110ms and 260ms respectively.
[06:02] Tom: the incumbent's numbers were inconsistent across runs, do you think that's due to their autoscaler or their kernel selection?
[06:09] Samira: likely kernel selection and suboptimal batching; their runtime doesn't do continuous batching across GPUs as efficiently, plus their routing had more cross-zone traffic in our setup which increased latency.
[06:21] Devon: action: we'll re-run e2e from our staging with production network paths and send logs.
[06:26] Alex: perfect. last part — decisions and next steps. we recommend two immediate items: 1) run your E2E test with prod traffic pattern 2) we prepare a dedicated slot proposal and pricing.
[06:37] Tom: agreed. one question — what's the rollback/fallback if we see an accuracy regression during rollout?
[06:44] Samira: we have automatic canary checks; if eval metrics drop beyond threshold we automatically revert traffic to the previous version or to incumbent fallback depending on your routing policy.
[06:55] Maya: that's reassuring.
[06:57] Alex: ok I'll recap in the notes. thanks all.
[07:01] (meeting closing chatter, small talk)
